sections.h2: Where is Troup County and what shapes its housing?
sections.html:
Troup County sits on Georgia's western edge against the Alabama line. LaGrange serves as seat of government and is the largest city. Of 446 square miles, 414 are land, and the Piedmont terrain runs through all of it. Interstate 85 and Interstate 185 cross the county, with U.S. 27 and several state routes, so Atlanta commuters and Columbus-area workers both choose to live here. Heard, Coweta, Meriwether and Harris counties adjoin it, and so do Chambers and Randolph counties in Alabama.

The General Assembly drew the county lines on June 9, 1826, once Creek land cessions opened the area, per Wikipedia's county entry. Cotton mills built around LaGrange in the late 1800s anchored local work for generations. Textile jobs eventually moved overseas, and auto parts suppliers serving the nearby Kia plant took up some of the slack. West Point Lake and Callaway Gardens bring in visitors.

Incorporated places are LaGrange, Hogansville and West Point. Long Cane, Mountville, Harrisonville and Abbottsford are unincorporated communities. A bungalow in LaGrange, a lakeside lot near West Point and a farm tract outside Hogansville attract quite different buyers, and each can come with its own tax history. Troup County School District runs the public schools, and a commission with a countywide chairman plus four district members governs.

sections.h2: How many people and homes does Troup County have?
sections.html:
Census estimates for mid-2025 put Troup County at 72,844 people, which is 4.9% above the April 2020 base. Roughly 61 of every 100 housing units are lived in by their owners, and QuickFacts lists the middle owner-occupied value at $217,200.

Decennial counts climbed from 50,003 in 1980 to 58,779 in 2000 and 67,044 in 2010. In 2020 the county tallied 28,721 housing units, 8.4% of them empty, and about four in ten occupied units were rentals. Seniors account for 17.8% of residents, so inherited houses and estate sales appear regularly.

sections.h2: Which Troup County office does what?
sections.html:
Your tax passes through two separate desks. One collects money. The other, a citizens board served by the Property Appraisal Department, decides what the parcel is worth.

  • Tax commissioner: (706) 883-1620, open on weekdays from 8 to 5, for bills, mobile home and timber tax, and tag renewals.
  • Property Appraisal: (706) 883-1625, at 100 Ridley Avenue, Suite 2100, LaGrange, for values, returns, exemptions and appeals.
  • Superior Court clerk: where deeds and tax liens are recorded.

The county's appraisal FAQ describes the assessors as a part-time citizens board, so a call may land on voicemail and be returned later. That board picks the Chief Appraiser, answers to state law and the Georgia Constitution, and gets its budget from the county commission. Card and online payments run through a county portal with a Property Taxes choice, and the tax office also takes payment by phone.

sections.h2: When are Troup County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Troup's property tax page names November 15 as the official deadline, with penalties and interest piling up after it. State revenue officials let counties move the statewide default, so read the date printed on the bill you actually receive.

Georgia freezes market value as of January 1 and then taxes 40% of it. Millage comes from the school board, the county governing authority and any other body that covers your parcel. A sample calculation on the appraisal FAQ uses .030260 as the rate and takes off exemptions first. Mobile homes and timber reach the same collector on their own timetables.

  • The state ratio is 40%, applied to market value.
  • One mill means a dollar per thousand dollars of assessed value.
  • A higher value or a dropped exemption can lift a bill while the rate stays flat.

sections.h2: What is the route for disputing a Troup County value?
sections.html:
Appeals grow out of the yearly assessment notice, and you get 45 days after the notice date shown on its face. Once that passes, you lose the chance to challenge that year's number.

The appraisers say they want sales records, photos of similar houses that changed hands lately, and whatever else supports your figure. A Board of Equalization hearing usually follows. Grand jurors name its members, who are neighbors and fellow owners, and filing is free. Arbitration is the other lane: each party hires one arbitrator and splits a third. Going on to Superior Court adds a $25.00 filing fee, per the county FAQ.

After a board or court rules, the assessors cannot move that value for two years without walking the parcel themselves.

sections.h2: Do LaGrange, Hogansville and West Point send separate bills?
sections.html:
Possibly. State revenue officials explain that a city levies its own ad valorem tax and that its clerk bills and collects it, unless the city and county have agreed to one combined statement. Troup's county pages do not say which arrangement applies to each of its three cities, so ask the tax commissioner at (706) 883-1620 and the clerk of your city before you assume one payoff covers everything.

The same state page gives taxpayers at least 60 days from the postmark of a bill before interest starts. A parcel inside city limits can therefore owe two separate payoffs at closing, one to the county and one to City Hall, and each may carry its own due date. Collect both figures in writing.

sections.h2: Which Troup County exemptions are worth a look?
sections.html:
Homestead filings are taken from the first of January through April 1. Miss the window and you forfeit the benefit for that year. Property Appraisal at (706) 883-1625 hands out the forms and quotes the amounts.

Other special exemptions are kept in the same office. The state's county facts page adds two quirks: skipping a return means you are deemed to have returned the same property at last year's final value, and freeport relief for inventory needs a local vote. A move means filing again for the new address.

  • Own the house and live in it on January 1.
  • A refund claim for a tax wrongly assessed has a three-year limit from payment.
  • Mobile homes sit on a separate location permit and return cycle.

sections.h2: How should a Troup County seller handle the tax bill?
sections.html:
Ask the collector for a payoff amount ahead of scheduling the closing, and let the attorney or title agent pay it from what you receive. Each year's bill goes to whoever held title on January 1, so an October sale can still leave a statement in your mailbox unless the settlement sheet divides the tax.

The tax commissioner's news page posts a courtesy tax sale list and a note that excess funds after such a sale go only to the record owner at that time or to other lienholders. A home that spent years as a rental, an estate asset or an empty shell may owe for several years, so request every year's status in writing.

A cash buyer can still close while a balance is open, because the payoff is deducted at the table. Set the closing statement next to the payoff letter and compare each line.

faqs.q: How do I phone the Troup County tax office?
faqs.a: The number is (706) 883-1620. Questions about value or exemptions go to Property Appraisal at (706) 883-1625.

faqs.q: Is November 15 the Troup County payment deadline?
faqs.a: Yes. The county tax page calls November 15 the official deadline and says penalties and interest follow it. Confirm against your own statement.

faqs.q: How long can I challenge a Troup County assessment?
faqs.a: Forty-five days after the notice date. A late filing forfeits the right for that year, and appeals cannot be filed without a notice.

faqs.q: When does Troup County take homestead applications?
faqs.a: From New Year's Day through April 1. Anything filed later waits for the next year.

faqs.q: Who owes the tax if I sell in October?
faqs.a: The person who owned it on January 1 is billed. Pay it at closing, after getting the payoff letter from the tax commissioner.
